utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. And good morning to you, Madam Registrar. If you could kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci. All the accused are here. From the Defence teams I only notice the absence of Mr. Meek. Also see some new faces. The Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. We have been told that there are some preliminaries that you would like to raise. I think from the Prosecution. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just wanted to update you on the week's witnesses briefly. We have based on -- we've shaved some time off, you may have noticed that I went for half an hour and we estimated an hour and a half. The Defence went for three and a half hours less than they'd estimated. And the estimates for this witness on the Defence were originally five, but they are now saying that that's going to be significantly less. We've had to postpone Witness 139 so after Lazarevic, we have one more witness, a MUP witness. Of course we'll have to see how it goes but that's the way the week looks. The MUP witness got here just recently so if we do finish Lazarevic earlier than anticipated, we'll need to start the MUP witness tomorrow first thing in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And how long do you expect that witness to be testifying, including cross? Will it cover us Friday too or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think it will. Because it's hard to say but the estimates for him are not -- are not that long. I don't have that right at my finger trips, but I don't think it was more than an hour and a half on direct and it's mostly a witness that the Borovcanin --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And then there is two hours 20 minutes, out of which one hour is from the Borovcanin team. I don't expect it to be much longer. Anyway, we have to play it by the ear -- play it by ear and see how it goes. Thank you. Anything else? Last week, we issued an order in relation to the trial lengths, in view of a possible joinder, and we haven't -- you haven't come back to us as yet, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm working on that right now, as well as our people, Mr. Thayer and others, and we're trying to get that as organised and as accurate as we can. I can -- I'll talk to Mr. Thayer at the break and see if we can give you an idea when we will be able to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The other thing is we discussed this morning, and we believe that we should bring this to your attention, because so far it has been contained only in a letter that Accused Tolimir sent to me and to the Registrar, a handwritten note dated 19th June, which is a few days ago but which was communicated to me yesterday. And basically, in it -- I don't think I should read it all, but basically, in it, Accused Tolimir, referring to the joinder motion, is on his own initiative proposing that the Trial Chamber dismiss the Prosecution motion on joinder of the case and he gives various reasons for that. He believes that through separate cases and proceedings, an adequate distribution of time for his preparation would be ensured and that separate proceedings would be ensured in a much shorter period of time. And lastly he says that he will define other reasons after permanent counsel has been assigned to him. It's my understanding also that there has been some progress in assigning counsel to Mr. Tolimir and you know that there will be a further initial appearance on Tuesday where we suppose the situation would crystallise. So that is the position at the moment. However, between now and then, we will be handing down a ruling establishing time limits for the filing of responses in relation to the two motions, the motion for joinder in the respective two cases. Expect that tomorrow. All right. There are no further preliminaries, I take it. Then we can bring in Mr. Lazarevic and proceed. And thank you for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good to see you back and ready to continue testifying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye? Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, good morning to you. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lazarevic. Yesterday when we left off last you had been talking about information that had been given to you by your commander. I just want to clarify for the record where was it that this information was conveyed to you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the command in Malesici.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you recall, was there anybody besides yourself present when your commander related this information to you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose there must have been, but I don't know their names. I'm sure there must have been people, but I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as best as you recall, about how long after your commander had initially gone to go home did he give you this information?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he returned from Rocevic, he told us all that. I don't know how late it was. I'm sure that it was in the afternoon but I don't know exactly when it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that. Now, when he returned from Rocevic and you had this conversation, what did he do following the conversation?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a conversation with him. He was telling us all that. It is not that I specifically had a conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What happened after he told you all of that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kozluk, we had a place where he called us by the telephone. He asked for Pandurevic and Obrenovic and he couldn't get them. And then he called the brigade again. He spoke to somebody and he says that he had spoken with a security man from the corps and that he was told that on the following day these people would be exchanged. I don't know who he spoke to. He only said that he spoke to the security guard from the corps. That's the only thing that he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Just based on the rate of the interpretation I've received, maybe you could just slow down just a little bit so that we can make it a little easier on the interpreters as well. Now --

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You made a reference to Kozluk. Were you in Malesici when you got this information?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So my question to you is what did he do following he gave -- following his giving you this information while you were in Malesic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you that he called by the phone that he asked for Pandurevic and Obrenovic, but he could not get in touch with them. After that, he again called the brigade and he got in touch with a security guy from the corps and that security guy had promised him that these people would be exchanged on the following day. And this is all I can tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. What happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I believe that we went to bed. I don't know what happened next. At that moment, nobody made a record of the course of events. We went to bed and sometime around midnight, maybe around midnight or 1.00 or 2.00 after midnight, a phone rang and the telegram arrived. This is what I stated and this is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Tell us about this telegram that arrived.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The telegram arrived, and in that telegram, it was requested that a group of people would be sent to Rocevic to execute these men. The telegram was coded. We could not decode it and signals guys came to decode the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you actually see this telegram?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all saw it, all the telegrams that arrive, there was a notebook by the induction telephone and the telegrams were recorded. We all saw the telegram but we could not decode it and then the signals guys came, decoded it and then we all knew what the content of the telegram was. We could not read it before these guys came.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How did you come to know of the telegram in the first instance?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who received it. It could have even been me. I don't remember the details. In the building where the telephone was, three people would bed there. It was not always the same people. So I don't know who received that telegram. It could have even been me but I'm not sure. One of the three guys received the telegram, one of the three who slept in that room by the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you saw the telegram, was it in a coded form or in a decoded form?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was coded. The signals guys came, and they decoded it as I've just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know who the signals guys were that came to decode the telegram?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the guys who were signals guys, but I don't know which one of them actually decoded it. I wouldn't be able to tell you that. I knew all of them. I knew who they were. But which one of them decoded that particular telegram, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of what the telegram said, did you have an opportunity to see that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us who were in the command read the telegram and I was one of them, one of those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So you read it after it had been decoded?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We all saw it. We all knew the content of the telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What do you recall that the content of the telegram was?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That a group of men from the 2nd Battalion should be allocated for the job of executing these people who were accommodated in Rocevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was this information communicated to your commander?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. He was the first to receive all the information, and then he would be the one to decide who would do what, to assign different tasks based on the information that he received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Tell us what happened after this information was communicated to your commander.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander refused to carry out the order and all of us who were there supported him in his decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Who was there?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, and you asked me yesterday, I don't know exactly who was there but I suppose that everybody who was at the command was there, even the company commanders were there during the night when all this happened. Yesterday I told you who the people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Was there any discussion about what to do concerning this telegram, involving the commander and the others in the command?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say the other commanders?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The other members of the command and the commander.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, of course. At that moment, we were all of the opinion that only somebody who was not normal could have issued such an order and after that, the commander sent a telegram back to the brigade refusing to carry out the order that he had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, did you see that telegram as well?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, because it was sent from the same induction telephone, a telegram was sent to the brigade refusing to carry out the order that we had received. I don't know under which number that telegram was sent but of course I saw it. It was sent from that same telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Are you saying it would have been in the same book as the order -- as the telegram that was received?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Because everything that was received from the brigade would be recorded in a notebook, and at the same time, whatever we sent back to the brigade would be recorded in the same notebook as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, was that telegram sent back -- that was sent back to the brigade, was it coded as well?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I don't know whether it was coded or not. I know it was sent but whether it was coded, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall in substance what the telegram said with respect to the refusal that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the wording. I know that the order was refused and that's the essence of the whole thing. I don't know exactly how it was worded, but I know that the gist of the telegram was that the order was being refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was rather inartful, but what I would like to know is if you can recall if there was a reason that was proffered for the refusal.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was that the order was just crazy, and at that moment we mustered the courage to say that our battalion was not prepared to carry out such an order, and that's where my interest in the matter stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was there any discussion of this issue with the infantry company commanders?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the commanders of the companies and all the other members of the command were familiar with the order and the reaction to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what happened after this telegram was sent in response to the one that was received from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the commander was shouting, he was talking to somebody, I don't know with whom, and he was cursing and quarrelling with somebody, but I don't know who that was. Our commander was a very quiet and self-effacing person and he would never volunteer any information unless you specifically asked for it. I know that he had words with somebody, that he was talking quite loudly, but I don't know who he was talking to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just to put this in context, is this somebody that you're referring to that was in the command or somebody that was not in the command?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know. He was talking to at the command. He could not quarrel with the command. He could only talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Again, maybe my question is inartful. I mean when I say command, I'm talking about somebody in Malesici or not in Malesici?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Malesici.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he quarrelled with somebody who was not in Malesici.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did that conversation occur over the telephone or by some other means?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did you have any indication as to whom he might have been talking to while you were -- while this quarrelling and cursing was going on?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, I suppose we went to bed, and any way, if we hadn't, it would have been a different course of events. I think we went to bed straight after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether or not any other telegrams were sent, either to or from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the telegram that you saw that was received from the brigade, did you understand that to be an order or a request?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the army there are no requests. There are only orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, as far as the next day is concerned, do you recall what transpired?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the commander went to Rocevic to tell them he would not select men for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. First, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he told us. We talked in the morning and the discussion was about his going to Rocevic to tell them that he was not going to detach people for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he go alone or did he go with somebody?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alone, as far as I know. I think he went alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you aware of whether or not any other members of the 2nd Battalion went to Rocevic that day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And after the commander went to Rocevic, did you receive any information about what was going on at the school?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that time, we up there who were on the front line didn't know a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Did you at some point later find out what was going on at the school that day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, word got out later, after a while, that those people had been taken away by trucks. I don't know whether it was one or two or three days later. In any case, they were taken away from Rocevic by truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you know whether or not the 2nd Battalion had volunteered any trucks or used any trucks in that process?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the start of the Srebrenica operation, a request came -- a demand came from the brigade that all units who had trucks should send those trucks with drivers to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And was that done with respect to your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how many trucks or drivers were sent to the brigade by your battalion?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only one driver and one truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall the driver, the name of the driver that was sent?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning. Just we've had these names were mentioned previously in closed session with the previous witness, and I believe that it will be better to have these names and this part of the examination-in-chief of my colleague performed in closed session. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. In fact, we need to redact line 13, the name line 13 and if we are going to proceed on this area of testimony, we need to do that in private session, if we are going to mention names.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I only have maybe a couple of questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- and I'll be out of this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session, then, please. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the events that transpired at the school involving these prisoners, were you ever at the school yourself, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to be a pupil at that school because that's a neighbouring village to mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Specifically to the time period that we are talking about, though, were you ever at the school?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I told you a hundred times that I hadn't been there then. You're asking me these questions -- no, no. No way. At that time we were all on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Bear with me for one moment. All right. Mr. Lazarevic, I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Also for sticking to the time frame that you had indicated before. Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be the first one going up asking questions in cross-examination for this witness, but giving the answer that was just provided by the witness, I'd like to have a short break simply to reorganise my notes and my -- maybe shorten my cross-examination after I speak with my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much time you require.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Ten minutes, 15 minutes at the most, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a ten minute break. If you require more time, just let us know in the meantime, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. --- Break taken at 9.39 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, M. Bourgon. S'il vous plait.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My name is Stephane Bourgon and I'm the counsel representing Drago Nikolic in this case, but I guess you know that already because we met yesterday, right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I have quite a few questions for you concerning your testimony, as well as the interviews you provided with the Prosecution before testifying today. First I'd like to begin simply by confirming that your initial interview with the Prosecution took place on 27 June 2002. Do you recall this date or the approximate --

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yeah. Around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: This took place in Banja Luka, and I think you remembered that the name of -- I'm sorry I may have cut you off. So this took place in Banja Luka, you remember this?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you remember that the name of the investigator or do you remember by any chance the name of the investigator was Mr. Bursik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, although I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I have with me of course the transcript of that interview, and we may have to refer to that during your testimony today. My second question is that do you remember meeting with some persons representing the accused Drago Nikolic on 29 May of this year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recall that. That was in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'd also like to confirm with you that last week you met with the counsel for the Prosecution. The date I have is 20 June. So I guess that would be last Thursday; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you mentioned at the beginning that, of course, you recall that you and I met yesterday for a few minutes, just before you began your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you remember, of course, most of the information that you provided to -- whether the Prosecution or the Defence, at each of these interviews?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: One quick question before we continue is: Did you, after meeting with the Prosecution last week, did you meet with them again to discuss your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the Prosecutor? Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So when did you meet with them again?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I didn't meet with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, in the transcript it said "yes." I'm sorry, in the transcript it said, "Yes." Okay. Lets move on to my first area of question. Yesterday we discussed the style of command of your commander, Mr. Acimovic, and I'd simply like you to confirm that it is your view that Mr. Acimovic was, one, very young, that he had a limited education, but that he was also very brave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also mentioned to me of course that he was the type of commander that would go out of his way to accomplish any orders issued to him?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that about the commander Vinko Pandurevic. His orders he always tried to comply with and execute, but I didn't speak about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I move to another topic. During your testimony of course you discussed the presence of prisoners in the Rocevic school, and I'd just like to confirm with you that before that day, when your commander first told you about the presence of prisoners in Rocevic, this is something that you had no knowledge of whatsoever; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. I was in Malesic. How should I have known?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So this was a complete surprise and you had never heard before that day that there were prisoners to be distributed in various schools in the area of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was a surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it was also a surprise for anybody who was present at your battalion that day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I move to the situation in the battalion command on the night of 14 July, first, you've already mentioned and I'd like you to confirm that everyone was sleeping at the battalion command when the telegram you referred to arrived; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The phone woke us up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you yourself, I put that question to you when we met, you don't remember whether you were the officer on duty that night?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I've already answered that in reply to the Prosecutor's question. Somebody was on duty but 12 years after the event, how can I remember who it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what about Vujo Lazarevic? Do you remember whether he was on duty that night?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you I don't remember exactly. Why are you asking me that question again and again? If I can't tell you whether it was I, how can I tell you whether it was somebody else? I'm not sure who was on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Just to let you know, Mr. Lazarevic, whatever I asked you before, the Court is not aware of this, so we have to go through this exercise so that the Judges are aware of your answers.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. Ask me questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, also when we spoke yesterday you confirmed that the -- that conversation at the battalion command involving the telegram, you confirm that it involved more than three persons; although, you don't remember the names of the others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you and I told the Prosecutor that everybody is on the line, 100 per cent of the men were there, and all the command members were there as well. Whether there was somebody else, I really can't tell you. I can't remember all these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But the only thing I'm trying to -- I understand that you may not remember the names, but whether there was three or more people is something that I believe one would be able to remember, and yesterday you mentioned to me four or five, maybe six?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure there were more than three men there. I'm sure of that. I'm absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when those discussions took place concerning the telegram that you say arrived that night, I take it that you yourself are present in these discussions?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And as you told me yesterday, that from that point on, you were always in the command thereafter, in the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, can you confirm that throughout those events -- I'm talking about that night, and I include the activities of the morning -- can you confirm that your commander never mentioned the name Drago Nikolic in relation to this telegram?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you he only told us that he wanted to talk to either Pandurevic or Obrenovic. He never mentioned Nikolic. And I also told you that he is a man of very few words. He never volunteered the information. I never asked him who he had spoken to. Hence, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge of a telephone conversation between Drago Nikolic and your commander that night or in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any knowledge of that, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move now, Mr. Lazarevic, to the situation of the presence of prisoners at Rocevic school, and that's the information that you testified about yesterday and today. First I'd like to confirm with you that everything you know about Rocevic on the 14th of July is what was reported to you by your commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all I know. I've told you I only heard things from the commander. I did not see these people myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that was my next question, that you did not see anything yourself that took place in Rocevic either of these two days?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that conversation that you reported earlier today, you said that your commander made a phone call from Kozluk. This conversation of course, you did not hear that conversation, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said, and I repeat, that he always asked for Pandurevic or Obrenovic. I've stated that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you yourself, Mr. Lazarevic, did not speak to the priest that you mentioned yesterday in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned that your commander had a conversation with the priest in Rocevic. But you yourself never spoke to that priest?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could I have spoken to him? I was in Malesic, 30 kilometres away. How should I have spoken to the priest? I was not in Rocevic and the priest was in Rocevic. He organised with the priest for these men to be given food and water. What on earth did that have to do with me? I was in a different place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that's all I'm trying to do is just to confirm this for the record that you did not speak to the priest and that you would also agree that you did not speak to the president of the local community who spoke with your commander.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, how could I have spoken to him? I was 20 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, Mr. Lazarevic, you testified that your commander had been informed by his father and his mother about the presence of prisoners. Now, I refer here to the page 13366 of the transcript, yesterday's transcript, sorry, at lines 8 to 11.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And today, you confirmed -- both yesterday and today you confirmed that this happened in the afternoon. So your commander left for a shower in the afternoon and came back in the afternoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that you mentioned yesterday, and I refer to your answer at page 13367, lines 9 to 11, that your commander first saw the prisoners and later he talked with the priest and the president in order to provide some food and some water. That's what your commander told you about the events; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And your commander told you that the gym was full of prisoners. That's what you said yesterday at page 13367, lines 12 to 13.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm just -- I was just a bit surprised yesterday when you mentioned that because this is the first time that we hear that your commander was aware that the gym was full. So you -- I just want to confirm that you never mentioned this information before.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's just to establish the facts. Now, Mr. Lazarevic, yesterday at page 13367, line 17 to 18, you mention being told by your commander that security guards had killed a few people. You remember saying that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you also stated that on the same page, a little later, that you don't know if your commander saw this for himself, simply what he told you.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also stated yesterday that your commander told you about a woman who had been wounded by the guards keeping the prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And you also mentioned one last thing concerning that those guarding the prisoners had threatened your commander. That's what he told you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that from him. I can only confirm what I heard from him, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you just tell us, how is it that you never mentioned before the issue of the security guards killing a few people, the wounded woman, and the guards threatening your commander? This was never mentioned before.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever asked me about that. That's why.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I move on to the fact that your commander, when he came in, and I'll quote you now from your interview, and I can show it to you if necessary but I don't think it will be, you stated and that's the interview in English page 13 and 14 for my colleagues from the Prosecution, you stated, "And I know that he tried to talk to the commander, or Chief of Staff, but he couldn't, nobody was available. Then he talked to someone in the corps, and I know that there were sort of fights or a conflict because he was -- and gave it the -- that which was where had gone" that's basically -- I quote from your interview. If you recall, how did that take place when your commander arrives at the battalion command? Does he tell you about this conversation first or does he tell you what he saw in Rocevic first?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the sequence. You're asking me to remember things that I can't remember after 12 years. I've just told you everything I know. I can't remember the exact sequence of all these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And so basically, the -- of course, the -- your commander comes back to the battalion command and he gives this information to all those who are present. That's what you said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I've repeated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned this morning that then there was a conversation or a call made to the brigade. Is that one call in Kozluk or is there two calls, one in Kozluk and one at the battalion command? To the best of your memory.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the commander, he made a call from Kozluk, and I know that he made another one from the command, which means that he made two telephone calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the call that was made at the battalion command, you say you know of this phone call. Were you there beside the commander when he called or were you told about this call?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you he is not a man of many words, and I could not be with him at all times. I was not his baby sitter. I know that he made a call because he shouted down the telephone. I've already told you that. We could hear him shout down the telephone line, quarrel with somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And just to confirm that when he at that moment, during that conversation, when he was shouting, this conversation, you don't know who he was speaking to other than from what he told you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. He never told me. How was I supposed to know who was on the other end of that telephone line?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. I move to a different topic, Mr. Lazarevic. I mentioned to you yesterday I would ask you a few questions concerning the communications between your battalion and the brigade, as well as communications between your battalion and the companies. So I just have a few questions I'd like to ask you on this topic. First, can you confirm that the communications centre in your battalion was located about 40 metres away from the battalion command in a different building?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how many metres. In any case it was close. I don't know whether it was 40 metres, 100 metres, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But it's a different building?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that building is where the -- I'm not sure because of the translation how to call these people, I call them signalmen. Maybe I'll just try this word to see if you understand the translation?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yeah, yes, that's what I call them, I understand everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That's where the signalmen were working?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm that the communication between -- just one moment. I'm being told there is a translation error I need to check. Sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I'm ready to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I'll go on with the communications -- just general questions concerning communications. Can you confirm that the induction phone you testified about, that's a military secure line and this line exists between the battalion command and the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And that this is a secure line in the sense that conversations on this line cannot be intercepted unless you plug into the wire physically?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how things should be, but I'm not really familiar with that field, and I can't talk about it for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in your battalion command, you would agree with me that you also had a radio which was on a brigade network but this radio was very rarely used other than for radio checks at fixed times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say radio sets? Do you mean Motorolas or a proper radio set?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Maybe I'll break down the question just to make it easy and we understand each other. There was a proper radio set in the battalion command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there wasn't. There were just Motorolas, a civilian telephone line, and an induction telephone line. I'm not sure about this radio set that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And the Motorola, how often was it used and by whom?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The company commanders, the commander and the deputies had those. And they were used for their internal communication, the communication among themselves. Nobody else used them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you know yourself, Mr. Lazarevic, whether it was possible from the battalion to reach the brigade on the radio?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: As far as the communications between the battalion command and the companies and the battalion forward command post or IKM, communications were also ensured by this induction telephone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And are you aware that the companies also had an RUP 12 radio but that they did not use them other than just to make checks at some times?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I know that there were Motorolas, there was an induction telephone, and I don't know anything about the thing that you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can you confirm that the -- if you wanted to place a call using the induction telephone to the brigade, you would first have to call your communications centre, that was the signalmen?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You don't have to go on. Yes, the answer is yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then they called the switchboard at the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then the switchboard at the brigade connects to the -- whichever office you're looking for in the brigade command?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I move on now to the telegram that you testified about. And first I'd like you to come back to something you said in your interview, and I quote now from page 26 in English for my colleague from the Prosecution, and I'll just quote you and then ask you to explain further. You stated then, "There was a separate logbook for telegrams because this was -- this was notebook strictly laid by the telephone, and when the message would come, it was registered."

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you explain that a little more so that the Trial Chamber understands? Where is the book and where is the telephone in the command, and what's the procedure when a telegram arrives?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've answered it yourself. The notebook was by the telephone on a desk. How am I supposed to explain that? It was on the desk, in a corner, and when a telegram arrived, somebody received it and the commander would be informed about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry for asking these questions, but I understand that for you it's 12 years but for us we weren't there at all; and we are trying to picture ourselves in the battalion command. And I would just like to confirm that this book is immediately, first of all, beside the phone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've told you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And because you mentioned there was a separate logbook for telegrams, I take it that beside the phone there are two books?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, just one for all the messages that arrived from the brigade. There was just one notebook, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when a telegram arrived, did it arrive in writing, like through a machine, or some other -- some other way?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that once. You hold your telephone receiver in one hand and you use your other hand to jot down what you hear. I've already told you that, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure you mention it in your testimony, and if you did, I'm sorry, I just wanted to make that clear for everyone. But can you confirm whether you write down immediately in the book or on a piece of paper beside the book?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You always record it in the notebook. Whatever you heard on the telephone, you record it immediately into the notebook, as if it had been dictated to you down the telephone. You would take notes in the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And then who would dictate that to you? Would that be a signalman from the brigade or would that be the duty officer from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say anything to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And within the battalion command, who would note it down? Anybody who happens to pick up the phone or the duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes the duty officer, but in principle, it was whoever happened to be there. Not much was made of who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us, and assist the Trial Chamber, in explaining how does a coded telegram look like? What do you get over the phone exactly? What kind of information do they give you? Because we are not soldiers here, and we are just trying to see -- I get the telegram. How does it look like? What do I get over the phone?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I was not a soldier to tell you, and number 2, I don't know what a coded telegram looked like. I did not use the codes. I was not a signalsman. I was not aware of what this was all about. So don't ask me that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you did at time exercise the duty -- you were duty officer at times; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the duty officer in the battalion, the duty officer in the brigade, and the duty officer in the battalion are two different things. There is a distinction there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I don't want to confuse you. I'm talking that you yourself within the battalion command, you were at times the battalion duty officer, were you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you cannot confuse me, and second, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you received a telegram, all I'm trying to know is what is it that they mention on the phone so that we understand how these things work.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the contents of the message is relayed over the phone. I don't know what you're asking me. Whatever is dictated you write down. You take it to the commander, and he takes up the action from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And if the message is coded, what exactly do you get over the phone?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Numbers. I think it went using numbers. You're asking me about the means of communication. It was in coded text. They will you certain numbers, you write them down, and I really don't know how to explain it. That's a coded message.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But the coded message, because you mention in your testimony that you saw a coded telegram that night, and I'm just asking to you describe what it looked like. Did it have code words or coded numbers or coded characters?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember these things. There were numbers, I seem to remember, but I told you once already that it was the signalsmen who decoded such telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So you stated that that night those signalmen were called in to come and decode the telegram; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And were you there when they did that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was that done by one person or two persons?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall whether they used a book of codes?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So it is your testimony, however, that these signalsmen are qualified to decode telegrams?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since they worked there, they must have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I would agree, and I think you confirmed that but you never used in the first person, that you yourself were not able to decode a telegram; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, coded telegrams were rare, and second, I couldn't decode them. I told you that already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when you met with the Prosecution last week, you mentioned a few names for the first time, and these are names that you had mentioned to us before, and those are Miodrag Pisic, Goran Ilic, Dragan Stevanovic and Milisav Cvijetinovic. So do you know these persons?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the men in the signals unit, yeah, the signalsmen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And these persons or one of those persons would have been the one who came in, one or ones, if there was more, who would have come in that night to decode the telegram?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, that night there was also Vujo Lazarevic who was present. You mentioned that in your interview?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And is it possible that he decoded the telegram?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't ask me such questions. I told you already who decoded the telegram. Don't try to lead me to an answer that is not logical. It was the signalsman who decoded it, not Vujo, not I, not somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'm simply asking you, Mr. Lazarevic, could Vujo Lazarevic decode a telegram? Do you know if he could do that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you know whether your commander could decode a telegram?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you don't know, or no, he couldn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He couldn't. We didn't know how to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clearer. Mr. Bourgon, I'm told that we need to have a break in about five minutes' time so whenever it's convenient for you. If it's more convenient now, we'll have it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We could stop right now, Mr. President. I thought because we had a break maybe we could go on, but I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Whatever you decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm told that's the position. Can I ask you how much longer you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will stick with my initial estimate, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's an hour and a half. No, sorry, that's two hours. And the Popovic team?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I believe half an hour will be enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Beara?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: 15 minutes approximately, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no questions for this witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Gvero?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: Around 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can we have a 20 minute break instead of the usual 25? Is that agreeable with you, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Mr. Lazarevic. We'll try to finish as quickly as possible with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's relative, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Today, you mentioned that you saw the coded telegram. And I'd like you to try to remember whether you know who wrote the coded telegram in the book. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said already I don't know. Maybe even I did. I've said that once already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when you yourself arrive in the headquarters -- the command, sorry, headquarters is a word I'm used to. But when you arrive in the command, was the commander already there or did the commander come later?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't arrive. I was there, sir. I was there. I didn't go anywhere. The commander is the one who arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Because you referred earlier in your testimony that some people were already in the command because you slept there. That applies to you. You sleep in the command; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I mean, regularly, not just that night but as a regular procedure, you lived in the command during the war?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall how it is that you came about to take the book in your hand and to read the book?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the book. Don't ask me to remember something I can't remember. Everybody who was there knew about the telegram. I said that at the very outset. I don't know how else to explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, do you recall who gave the book to the commander so that he could read the telegram?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And do you recall when the signalmen came in, one or more, that we don't know, but when the signalmen came in, whether they decoded the telegram in the book or on a piece of paper beside the book?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you testified that coded telegrams were rarely received by the battalion command. What would have been the procedure, to write the decoded version immediately following the coded version in the book or separately?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know the details.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters request, could Mr. Bourgon please draw the microphone closer to himself?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Will do, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, when -- as part of your duties, because you describe your duties as being the officer for general affairs or assistant commanders for general affairs within the battalion command. Would I be right in saying that this book was part of your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So if anyone has told us that maintaining this book is part of your responsibilities, they were not correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody wrote in that book. I didn't keep that record. It's a simple notebook. It's not a logical question you're asking me. Nobody is in charge of that notebook. It's just there by the telephone. You jot down in it what you have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in your interview, and for the sake of my colleague I quote from page 15 in the English version, you stated the following: "I was not there when it arrived, but I -- my guess is that it came through the telephone and it was coded."

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what is in dispute here? I told you all I knew about it. Maybe I don't remember some details, but I told you all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, would you allow for the possibility that you did not see the telegram in the book because that's what you stated in your interview?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't ask me questions of this sort. I told you the telegram came, and yesterday when you asked me I told you about it. I don't know what other answer you want me to give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Well, in your interview, a little later on, you were again -- again you are asked a question and now I quote from page 27 for the sake of my colleague from the Prosecution, the question was, that's the investigator from the Prosecution asking you this question, "Did you ever see the telegram?" And your response was, "I didn't see it. But I know it was registered in the notebook and it was coded and I'm sure it was listed in the logbook." I'm simply asking you, do you allow for the possibility that you did not see the telegram in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot allow that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Then why is it simply -- can you explain why is it that you are mentioning this for the first time in this testimony that you saw the telegram when previously you told the investigators of the Prosecution that you had not seen it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember all the details, but I said yesterday and I'm saying again, the telegram arrived and everybody saw it. I don't know how many times I need to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I move on, today you were asked by my colleague from the Prosecution whether you had seen the decoded version of the telegram, and I think -- can you confirm that your answer was that you did not read the decoded version of the telegram? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the details. I know the contents of the telegram. The commander told us what it was about. I know the whole thing. What does it matter whether I saw it myself or not? I know the contents of the telegram. We all sat there at the command headquarters. We were talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And again when you say we all sat there, those are the four to six persons that you mentioned but you don't remember the names?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I told you who the members of the command were at the very beginning. I suppose all of them were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And just to confirm that you yourself are only aware of one telegram arriving from the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it is also your testimony that there was only of course one telegram sent from the battalion to the brigade; is that correct, in response?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, with regards to the company commanders, I take it that no copy of the telegram was sent to the company commanders. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: No meaning no copies were sent; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No copy because they too were at the command. Why would they send them a copy if they were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony yesterday, you mentioned the names of the three company commanders as being Dragan Stevanovic, Miroslav Stankovic and Milan Radic. I'd just like you to confirm that it is your testimony that they came to the battalion command that night to discuss this telegram; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not that the commander asked them. They were there, and he told them that the orders would be rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So just to clarify, were they there when the telegram arrived? I just want to clarify whether there was a request for them to come or did they just happen to be there?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander summoned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that they came to the command that night?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on to the response which was sent, you've already testified as to what the contents of the discussions were to the best of your recollection, but you don't recall who exactly sent the response, who picked up the phone to send the response in the form of a telegram?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was that telegram -- you've already testified that the telegram was -- you don't know whether the response was coded or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And was that telegram -- you've already testified that the telegram was -- you don't know whether the response was coded or not; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And would I be right in saying that that telegram was -- you don't know whether it was first written in the book, in the notebook, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that all telegrams that arrived would be noted down in the notebook. I don't know what other answer you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe my question was not clear. I'm talking about the telegram that was sent. It would also be the procedure to write this telegram in the book, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said everything that was received or sent would be noted down in that book.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: But you yourself did not see the response that was sent in the book that night. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember such things. I know that there was an order. It was an order. But I can't remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to refer to something which you mentioned in your interview again concerning the reason why your commander went to Rocevic in the morning. In your testimony today, you said that he went to Rocevic to let them know that they would not execute the order. Do you recall saying that this morning?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I remember. How could I not remember?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in your interview, and I quote from page 18 in English, you stated the following: The question posed to you was: "After discussion with the company commanders, what was the result of that?" And your response was, "I know that the following morning, our commander went to Rocevic." I'd just like to clarify that it is your testimony that the purpose or what led to your commander going to Rocevic is basically what the company commanders told him, "We have to get rid of those prisoners in the school," is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean "get rid of"? I've already said that everybody was on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Lazarevic. I noticed myself that the words used were not the best so I'm not talking about "get rid of". I'm talking of that the company commanders, they were from the Rocevic area, and they weren't happy with the fact that prisoners were in the school. So they basically were very much interested in ensuring that the prisoners would be moved from the school, and that's what they told to your commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I'm sorry if I used the wrong words. Now --

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never mind. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Regarding the trip that your commander made to Rocevic that morning, my colleague asked you how come you know that your commander went there and of course, he told you before going that he was going to Rocevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Of course. You're asking me things that have nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when your commander came back from Rocevic, would I be right in saying that he stated that he thought he would be called up to the court and punished for his act of disobedience? Is that part of what he mentioned to you when he came back?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And in this regard, your commander did not ask you to keep a copy of the telegram, just to protect him from future prosecutions against him?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, nobody was thinking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I'd just like to confirm that anything you know about the events which took place in Rocevic on that next day are what was mentioned to you by your commander and that you did not see any of that.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: If we can move into private session, Mr. President, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means. Let's go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I will ask that question once again because now we are back into public session. Knowing that your commander testified before this Tribunal last week, did you see him at all, either just before travelling to The Hague, in the days or weeks, or in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I saw him in passing before, but I saw him here at The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you discuss any of these events with him?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And did you discuss these events with anyone else?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And when I say anyone else, I'm talking the persons that were mentioned today or that were closely associated with the 2nd Battalion in July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in touch with anyone, as far as that is concerned. I'm not in touch with any of the people who have been mentioned because I work rather far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lazarevic. I have no further questions. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you first of all to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you introduce yourself, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Zoran Zivanovic, appearing in this case for Vujadin Popovic. My first question is: Could you clarify whether, in the building of the command where your battalion was quartered, you had a room to yourself where you worked?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic, can I ask you to repeat your answer, please? Because the interpreters didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always worked in a room right there in that building of the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were there several rooms in the building?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It used to be a big tavern. There was a big office space where we all worked and lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic and Mr. Zivanovic, please allow a pause between question and answer because we are heading straight to problems. Ms. Condon is usually very good at controlling you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One more thing: In addition to you, was there anyone in charge of those administrative affairs at the battalion?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Jovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague, Mr. Bourgon, showed you a document, and you said you were not the one who drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not, but I -- I know I didn't because it's not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now it's you, Mr. Lazarevic. Please allow a short pause before you answer Mr. Zivanovic's question. Don't jump straight with your answer even before he's finished putting his question to you, which is what you're doing. I will ask for your cooperation, which is very important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you maybe recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's Zoran Jovic. I think it's his handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, if you know, what that list was for?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, it was a fiction. You would put a name next to a name -- you would put a plus next to a name just in case there was somebody from the command to inspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if salaries were paid based on that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR LAZAREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Salary was paid to everybody who was mobilised, and the salary was 10, 20 deutschmark.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at one document, P312? And if we could move to private session, please.
